I've gotten another (internal) report of an identical crash, so I'm going to reopen this.

The internal report also gave me a full dump of the `.mypy_cache` from the crash.

The key thing of interest here seems to be that the module whose name appears in the KeyError message (a different one for our internal report) is not listed on the command line and hence does not get analyzed (because of `--silent-imports`).

Another observation: in the dump, a certain module (a _sibling_ of the KeyError module) was suppressed. But in the crashing run, that module was added to the command line. Hm....

OK, here's a repro.

```
rm -rf .mypy_cache a
mkdir a
cat >a/__init__.py <<EOF
from .b import B
from .c import C
EOF
cat >a/b.py <<EOF
class B: pass
EOF
cat >a/c.py <<EOF
class C: pass
EOF
mypy --silent-imports -i a/__init__.py
echo '#' >>a/c.py
mypy --silent-imports -i a/__init__.py a/c.py
```

The last line crashes with

```
KeyError: 'a.b'
```

Note that a/b.py is not checked, and it's not updated, but on the second run its name (`'a.b'`) somehow ends up in `deps`.

I also have a fix, just before the offending line in build.py (`stale_deps = ...`) insert

```
deps &= set(graph)
```

But I am not satisfied, because I don't understand the cause of the crash, I can just prevent it.

@Michael0x2a what do you think? Here's the test case:

```
[case testKeyErrorCrash]
# cmd: mypy -m a
# cmd2: mypy -m a a.c
# flags: --silent-imports
[file a/__init__.py]
from .b import B
from .c import C
[file a/b.py]
class B: pass
[file a/c.py]
class C: pass
[file a/c.py.next]
class C: pass
pass
```

**UPDATE the second:** The above test case reproduces the KeyError.

issue.title: Fix overzealous new submodule check
issue.body:
Fixes #2028?

Previously, when mypy detected a module acquired a new submodule after running mypy once in incremental, mypy would attempt to parse the module from scratch (if it hadn't already previously been parsed) which, as a side-effect, would find all of the child modules and load them as dependencies of the top-level module.

While this works in the usual case, this check made the flawed assumption that we would want to actually record/acknowledge every single new submodule that was created.

This assumption is not necessarily true when using --silent-imports -- it may be the case that we only want to record a _subset_ of the new submodules that were created, depending on what exactly the command line flags were.

body:
I _think_ I managed to isolate the error -- see https://github.com/python/mypy/pull/2189 for details.

I also wasn't sure why the test wasn't working, but it seems you figured it out? I can edit my pull request and copy in that test case, if you want.

**Edit**: I went ahead and added the test case.

I also think it might be worth explicitly documenting exactly what the expected behavior of doing something like `mypy some_module/__init__.py` vs `mypy --silent-imports some_module/__init__.py` is. 

As I understand it, the former is exactly equivalent to doing `mypy some_module` whereas the latter will make mypy typecheck only whatever's literally inside the `__init__.py` file and ignore all submodules. (I could be wrong, though -- if there's one thing I learned this summer, it's that imports are really tricky)

In any case, if you think this sort of thing is worth documenting, I can make another pull request to add this to the docs?

Thanks for the quick fix, and yes, I think documenting this more carefully would be helpful (there's already a longish section in `command_line.rst` about this. I think it's true that `mypy mod/__init__.py` is equivalent to `mypy -m mod`. But notice that `mypy -p mod` is very different: it locates the folder `mod` and explicitly (and recursively) adds any `.py` files it finds there, so all of them are impervious to `-s` (unlike with `-m`, where `-s` suppresses everything except `m/__init__.py`).

If you can turn that into orderly prose, please do!
PS. The reason my first few attempts at constructing a test failed were due to the way the test framework parses the "cmd" line -- apparently you can pass modules with `-m` but you cannot pass files.
